title: Shadows
coreIdea: Make the shadow the primary subject or an equal partner to the object that casts it.
whyItMatters: Shadows are pure graphic form and can function as secondary figures. Seeing them as content rather than byproduct changes how you use light and dramatically increases the number of usable frames in hard light. This is a core graphic skill shared by Cartier-Bresson, Erwitt, and many strong contemporary workers.
shootingBrief: Hard light conditions (high sun or strong low-angle sun). Look for human shadows on walls or pavement, architectural shadow patterns, shadows that create secondary figures or abstract forms. Minimum 8 frames where the shadow is essential. Experiment with including and excluding the casting object. Volume 40–70.
technicalFocus: Settings: Expose for the highlights if you want deep, graphic black shadows. Check the histogram.
Focusing: On the shadow plane or the casting object depending on which is primary.
Stance: Position relative to the light direction is critical. Small moves change the shadow dramatically.
Light: Hard, directional light only. Soft light kills the exercise.
Distance: Variable. Closer for abstract shadow forms; farther when the relationship between caster and shadow is the point.
Candid or pure shadow still life.
failureModes: Weak or soft shadows.
Including too much of the casting object so the shadow becomes secondary.
Busy ground or background that breaks the shadow shape.
Exposing for the shadows and losing the graphic quality.

goodVsExcellent.excellent: The shadow is more interesting or more complete than the object, or the two form a single graphic idea that neither has alone.

title: Reflections
coreIdea: Use reflective surfaces to create layered or doubled realities and deliberately control the mix of reflection and direct view.
whyItMatters: Reflections multiply information in a single frame and introduce controlled ambiguity. Mastery of them expands what one position can contain and is a major tool in the work of Saul Leiter, Vivian Maier, and Gustavo Minas. It also trains precise positioning — tiny changes in angle completely rewrite the content.
shootingBrief: Windows, puddles, polished metal, mirrors, wet pavement. Decide whether the reflection, the reflected subject, or the interaction between both is primary. Minimum 6 intentional reflection frames. Volume 40–70. Try both clean and fragmented reflections.
technicalFocus: Settings: Watch exposure carefully — reflective surfaces often trick the meter.
Focusing: On the reflection plane or the key subject within the reflection.
Stance: Tiny changes in angle and height completely change what is reflected. Work slowly.
Light: Angle relative to the reflective surface is everything.
Distance: Often closer work than usual.
Candid. Control or eliminate your own reflection unless it is a deliberate part of the picture.
failureModes: Uncontrolled self-reflection.
Muddy mix of reflection and reality with no hierarchy.
Weak or dirty reflective surfaces that add nothing.
Focusing on the wrong plane so the key information is soft.

goodVsExcellent.excellent: The reflection and the direct view create genuine visual tension or a new meaning that neither element has alone. The frame feels complex but resolved.

title: Doubles
coreIdea: Find or wait for visual pairs — similar shapes, postures, gestures, or forms that echo each other inside the frame.
whyItMatters: Visual rhyme creates instant structure and often humor or tension. It trains coincidence recognition and the ability to hold a frame open until the second element arrives. This is central to Elliott Erwitt’s best work and to Matt Stuart’s strongest coincidences.
shootingBrief: Pairs: two people with similar posture, matching shapes between architecture and human form, repeated gestures, twin objects. The double must feel intentional. Minimum 6 clear double/pair compositions. Volume 40–70. Timing is usually critical when people are involved.
technicalFocus: Settings: Shutter fast enough for gesture.
Focusing: On the plane of the critical pair.
Stance: Position so both elements sit in clear relationship. Longer end of the zoom often helps compress and emphasize the rhyme.
Light: Even or side light so both elements read with similar weight.
Distance: Medium working distance is common.
Candid. Patience for the second element to appear or align is the method.
failureModes: Accepting near-misses as doubles.
Pairs that are too dissimilar to create real rhyme.
Clutter that hides the relationship.
Shooting before the second element has fully arrived.

goodVsExcellent.excellent: The echo is precise, the rest of the frame supports the relationship without distraction, and the double creates tension or humor that elevates the picture.

title: Empty
coreIdea: Photograph urban emptiness and quiet so that absence itself becomes the subject.
whyItMatters: Most street photographers only feel competent when people are present. Empty frames force reliance on light, geometry, atmosphere, and precise framing. This builds formal strength and the ability to make a complete picture from limited content — a skill that improves every other day.
shootingBrief: Early morning streets, closed shops, vacant lots, quiet alleys, deserted platforms, empty benches. Make the emptiness feel intentional and atmospheric. Minimum 6 frames that successfully convey emptiness or solitude. Volume 30–50. Light and geometry must carry the picture.
technicalFocus: Settings: Can use lower shutter speeds if the scene is completely static.
Focusing: On the strongest geometric or light plane.
Stance: Precise framing. Edges and corners matter more when content is sparse.
Light: Directional light or interesting sky is often essential. Flat light makes emptiness look merely empty.
Distance: Often wider to emphasize the scale of the emptiness.
No people, or only distant and clearly secondary.
failureModes: Boring emptiness (just nothing happening).
Weak light.
Poor edge control and messy corners.
Including small distractions that break the sense of absence.

goodVsExcellent.excellent: The emptiness has mood, the frame feels complete and deliberate, and the picture would be weaker if a person were added.

title: Objects
coreIdea: Treat ordinary urban objects as the primary subject with the same seriousness you give people.
whyItMatters: Objects carry atmosphere, social information, humor, loneliness, and graphic power. Learning to see them as subjects expands your range and improves still-life seeing on the street. It also trains you to use light and context rather than relying on human expression.
shootingBrief: Chairs, signs, barriers, discarded items, street furniture, temporary structures, objects left behind. Minimum 8 frames where an object or small group of objects is clearly the subject. Volume 40–60. Context and light matter — avoid pure product shots.
technicalFocus: Settings: f/4–8 depending on desired depth.
Focusing: Precise on the object.
Stance: Get closer when it strengthens form and presence. Watch backgrounds and edges carefully.
Light: Side light or hard light reveals texture, volume, and character.
Distance: Often closer than typical people work.
Human presence only if it serves the object story.
failureModes: Product-style shots with no atmosphere or context.
Weak light that makes the object look ordinary.
Cluttered surroundings that compete.
Choosing objects with no visual or emotional charge.

goodVsExcellent.excellent: The object feels charged — lonely, funny, graphic, or socially revealing — and the frame supports that reading through light, context, and precise framing.
